question: Did California's AB 1228 minimum wage for workers at large limited-service restaurant chains ($20 per hour from 1 April 2024; signed 28 September 2023) change employment in California's limited-service restaurants (NAICS 722513) over its first eight quarters, 2024Q2-2026Q1, relative to limited-service restaurants in other states, and did the effect change between the first and the second year, when the policy's bite fell? The published QCEW-based studies disagree (Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen, NBER w34033 revised 2026: a decline of about 3.5%; Dube, NBER w35171, 2026: near zero). This is a pre-specified update of a contested question, not a new question: the latest published QCEW window ends in 2025Q4 (Clemens et al., w35931), so the data add one preliminary quarter, 2026Q1; the 2026Q2 release is due on 2 December 2026 and the crew does not wait for it.
hypotheses: H1 (first stage, in weekly earnings): the pooled 2024Q2-2026Q1 ATT on log average weekly wage (QCEW weekly earnings per job, not the hourly wage the law sets; fewer hours would bias it toward zero) of California NAICS 722513 relative to the comparison group, with the primary estimator fixed at the design gate, is positive: one-sided test at 5%. The inference method must be valid with a single treated state (Ferman-Pinto, conformal, or a permutation whose comparison pool is large enough that a 5% test is attainable without California ranking first by construction); standard errors clustered by state are not used. The design gate shows that the chosen pool and method attain the stated level. Reported also for each year separately, because the $20 fast-food wage did not rise in 2025 or 2026 while California's general minimum did (its premium fell from $4.00 to $3.10). If H1 fails, H2 is reported as uninformative about the wage floor.

H2 (main): the pooled 2024Q2-2026Q1 ATT on log employment of California NAICS 722513, same estimator and inference. Decision rule, fixed now, with b = 0.02 log points: compute the two-sided 95% CI [L, U] and the 90% CI [l, u] (a two one-sided test at 5%) with the H1 inference method. Sign: 'negative' if U < 0, 'positive' if L > 0, else 'sign undetermined'. Size: 'smaller than b' if -b < l and u < b, 'at least b' if u < -b or l > b, else 'size undetermined'. The headline label is the pair, in this exhaustive and mutually exclusive table: (negative, at least b) = 'decline of at least 2%'; (negative, smaller than b) = 'decline smaller than 2%'; (negative, size undetermined) = 'decline, size not distinguishable from 2%'; (sign undetermined, smaller than b) = 'no effect as large as 2%'; (sign undetermined, at least b) = 'inconclusive'; (sign undetermined, size undetermined) = 'inconclusive'; and the positive cases symmetrically ('increase of at least 2%', 'increase smaller than 2%', 'increase, size not distinguishable from 2%'). The bound: at the pooled log weekly-wage effect of about 7% that Dube (2026, Table 1 Panel A, SDID, the same pooled post-period estimand) reports, -0.02 is an own-wage elasticity of about -0.29, the size of the more negative published estimates; a CI inside +/-0.02 therefore separates the two published readings. The design stage computes, from pre-2023Q4 data only, the minimum detectable effect at 80% power, and the paper reports it next to H2. Timing for H1-H3, fixed now: the base period is 2023Q3, the last quarter before the law was signed; 2023Q4 and 2024Q1 (between signing and the effective date) enter neither the base nor the pooled post-period and are reported separately as a report-only anticipation estimate, as Sosinskiy and Reich (2026, Table A3) already report them; Dube (2026, Table 1 Panel B), whose base is the 2022Q1-2023Q3 mean so that 2023Q4 stays out of it, is the published result closest to this timing and is named as such in the paper; Dube's 2023Q4 base is a pre-specified robustness check, not an alternative primary. Choice of the primary specification, fixed now because the published literature already maps each choice to its result (w35931; Dube 2026, Table D1) and the PI has read that map: the design gate does not pick the estimator, detrending, outcome normalization, comparison pool or fitting window by judgement. The Designer lists a candidate set covering both published approaches (at least: DD and DD with a state-specific linear trend fitted on the pre-period, each on log employment and on log employment per capita; synthetic control; SDID; with the comparison pools both studies use), and the primary is the candidate with the smallest root mean squared error of placebo-in-time pooled ATTs at pseudo-treatment dates that use only data before 2023Q3 (the pseudo-dates, their windows and the tie-break are fixed in the design). Two named secondary analyses are reported whatever the rule picks: Clemens et al.'s detrended indexed DD and Dube's SDID, both re-estimated with the 2023Q3 timing above. The study is therefore pre-specified but not blind, and the paper says so.

H3 (reduced-form year two minus year one): the ATT on log employment for 2025Q2-2026Q1 minus that for 2024Q2-2025Q1, same estimator and inference, reported next to the yearly H1 wage effects (and the implied yearly own-wage elasticities), because the policy's bite fell in year two and a change cannot be attributed to time alone. 'Larger decline in year two' if the 95% CI of the difference is below 0, 'smaller decline in year two' if above 0, otherwise 'no detectable change'. If the pre-period MDE of the difference exceeds 0.04 (twice b), H3 is reported as uninformative whatever the estimate.
contribution: A pre-specified (not blind) update with modest novelty, stated as such: the estimand, base period, a rule that picks the primary estimator from pre-2023Q3 data only, inference valid with a single treated state and decision rules are fixed and reviewed before any post-2023Q3 outcome is computed; H2 adds an equivalence test against a 2% bound that separates the two published readings; H3 compares year two with year one next to the yearly wage effects, because the fast-food premium over California's general minimum fell from $4.00 to $3.10; the data add one preliminary quarter (2026Q1) to the latest published window (2025Q4). Decompositions of the published disagreement (Dube 2026, Tables D1-D2; Clemens et al. w35931, Table A1; Sosinskiy and Reich 2026, Appendix A) and published anticipation and base-period checks (Dube 2026, Table 1 Panel B; Sosinskiy and Reich 2026, Table A3; w35931, footnote 5) are cited, not repeated as findings. The PI and the Scout know the published estimates (disclosed); the analysing roles compute nothing on post-period outcomes before the design gate. Limits known now: QCEW counts jobs and weekly earnings, not hours or hourly wages; part of NAICS 722513 is outside the law's coverage (the published 70% coverage figure refers to 722513 and 722515 together; the share for 722513 alone is not known), so effects on covered jobs are diluted by an unknown factor; some covered chains sit in NAICS 722515, which therefore cannot serve as a control; county cells are suppressed more often from 2025, so the design must say whether the analysis is at state or county level; 2026Q1 is preliminary and will be revised.

tasks.title: Novelty and prior-estimate check: find every study of AB 1228's employment effects (at least Clemens, Edwards and Meer 2025; Dube NBER w35171 2026; Reich and Sosinskiy 2024 or later), record for each the data, period, estimator, comparison group, outcome definition and the headline employment estimate with SE, table and column; say whether any uses QCEW data past 2025Q3; list the specification choices on which Clemens et al. and Dube differ
Fetch QCEW industry slices 722513, 722511, 7225, 10 for 2014Q1 to latest; manifest; prepare county panel; CODEBOOK.md; no CA-vs-other or pre/post statistic

question.summary: AB 1228 eight-quarter effect on CA NAICS 722513 employment (H2, sign x size rule, b=2%), weekly-earnings first stage (H1), year two vs year one (H3); pre-specified not blind; one new preliminary quarter. Reviewer question-r4: pass; F15, F16 minor carried to the design stage.
